newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE-APEC a chance for Manila to boost, boast growth.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-APEC a chance for Manila to boost, boast growth.

text.p: The Philippines, already on a roll economically, hopes to use this month's APEC summit as a springboard to reaching the dream that has long eluded it of finally becoming one of the region's "tiger" economies.

"Hosting the APEC will enable us to have a role of leadership towards progressing the objectives of global trade, for our benefit," Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista told Reuters in an interview.
Bautista is co-chairman of a ministerial meeting which precedes the November 25 Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum leaders' summit in Subic, just north of Manila.

While neighbouring southeast Asian economies have been booming for years, the Philippines has only just begun to recover from a prolonged slump following 20 years of authoritarian rule under the late President Ferdinand Marcos.

The latter part of Marcos's rule until he was ousted in a popular revolt in 1986 was marked by political turmoil, followed by a series of natural calamities, which included the Mount Pinatubo eruption in 1991, the world's most powerful volcanic explosion this century.

The Philippines has staged what many economists regard as a remarkable comeback under current President Fidel Ramos, a workaholic former armed forces commander who has introduced a range of trade and investment liberalisation measures.
Key industries have been opened up to foreign competition, shaking up powerful local business interests who had long operated under strong state protection.
Ramos's whole approach to economic revival typifies what APEC is supposed to be about.

Leaders of the organisation's 18 member economies hold their summit on November 25 at the Subic freeport zone to map out a programme for removing all trade and investment barriers in the region, within 14 years for developed economies and 24 years for developing economies.
Top business executives will hold a parallel meeting to ensure the cooperation and support of the private sector.

APEC is a loose organisation of 18 economies -- Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, and the United States.
They contribute about 56 percent of the world's total gross domestic output and control more than 50 percent of world trade.

Assistant trade secretary Edcel Custodio, head of the Manila delegation at a series of APEC preparatory meetings, said hosting these events would showcase the Philippines' achievements and erase any lingering image that it was still "the sick man of Asia".
"We are hosting the APEC for a very selfish objective -- to project the Philippines in a different light," Custodio said.

In the first half of the year, the country's gross national product grew by more than 7.0 percent against 5.2 percent in the same period last year and against virtually flat growth when Ramos took office in 1992.

Exports have grown by an unprecedented 20 percent in the past three years, the highest growth rate in Asia. This year alone, the government expects export receipts to rise by 22.6 percent over last year's total of $29 billion.
Total exports are projected to reach $65 billion by the year 2000, or a growth rate of 25 percent in the next four years.
Even with its track record of the past few years, the Philippines sees intense competition from other nations and believes it cannot rest on its laurels.
"These targets need all the help they can get. We have to work hard for it... If we don't do anything in the next two years, our share in the market will be gone," Bautista said.
However, not everybody shares the government's view, and a vocal opposition says a free trade body like APEC allows large, economically powerful countries to dominate smaller nations.

"In our era of global transnational corporations, the partitioning of the world into various economic enclaves for the interests of monopoly capitalism has intensified, resulting in social disaster for millions of people," Edberto Villegas, former chairman of the University of the Philippines-Manila Division of Social Services, said in a report on APEC.
